Hello, Mrs Stevens. So I see here you were referred to the hospital by your GP.
Yes, but you can call me Marie.
Okay, so Marie, what was the initial reason you visited your GP?
Well, I went to my GP last week because over the last two weeks, well, I'm getting more and more yellow.
It's my skin and my eyes, basically.
I didn't think it was all that bad, but my husband said I was very yellow, especially the whites of my eyes.
And any other symptoms?
Yes, I'm also guessing a lot of tummy pain and it's been getting much worse.
So you said your husband first noticed the change in your skin. When was that exactly?
I think it was about 12 days ago when he said he first noticed something was wrong.
And you also mentioned experiencing tummy pain that is getting worse. Is the pain constant or does it come and go?
It is intermittent pain but I think it might be related to my bowels in general.
They have been a bit off lately.
What would you say has changed with your bowels?
I guess I really... a change in bowel movements.
They've been a weird colour recently, a bit pale, I guess you'd say.
And what about urinary output? Is that normal?
Output is normal, but my urine is definitely a lot darker than normal.
And going back to the tummy pain, where would you say the site of the pain is specifically?
It's here on my side.
Okay, so you're indicating your right hypochondrium.
And how long has it been going on?
It's been on and off for a few months now.
And what kind of pain is it?
I mean, is it a sharp or a dull ache?
Well, it can be quite sharp.
And when it's bad, it can just completely stop me in my tracks.
I mean, it can be so bad that I often feel nauseated when it's happening.
I mean, it was easy enough to ignore it at first because I'd get the pain every week or so.
But now I'm getting it at least one or two bouts a day.
So her dramatic uptick in frequency, does anything seem to trigger the pain or make it better?
I started noticing that if I eat a big dinner it'll get more painful.
I don't eat much at all now because it makes me sore and a bit nauseous.
Okay, so now I'm going to ask you a few questions about your past medical and surgical history.
Oh well, that's quite brief.
The only times I was ever in the hospital before today were for the birth of my two children
and for appendix surgery when I was a teenager.
And have you ever had a blood transfusion?
Not to my knowledge.
What about drug history?
Are you currently taking any regular medications?
I just take a blood pressure tablet.
Can't remember the name, but I've taken it for years.
Other than that, I don't take anything.
So you're not at risk for drug-induced jaundice.
As for my physical examination,
on palpation there are no masses,
but there is tenderness in the right upper quadrant.
So I'm going to order some investigations.
We need to get a full blood count, a liver function test,
as well as serum lipase and amylase so that we can rule out pancreatitis.
I'm also going to order a coagulation screen to assess the liver's synthetic function.
Imaging tests will also be needed,
but I will wait for the results of the other investigations before deciding which of these.
That sounds like an awful lot of tests. I mean, what do you think?

So, today we are going to review the major categories of strokes, which are ischemic and hemorrhagic.
There are several mechanisms related to the first classification, such as embolism, thrombosis, systemic hypoperfusion, and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.
All of these mechanisms reduce the blood supply to an area of the brain.
With the other category of strokes, there is a rupture in blood supply, such as with an intracerebral hemorrhage and subarachnoid hemorrhage.
So what I want to get into today is the Bamford classification of the first category of stroke.
The basis of this system is initial presenting symptoms and clinical signs.
It does not rely on imaging and is instead a purely clinical diagnosis.

So we've been having some issues with thorough documentation of chest x-rays lately,
so I just wanted to briefly cover the essential elements for documenting the results of this test.
So first it is necessary to write the date and indication for the chest x-ray,
such as patient presented with shortness of breath.
Then the next important component is the interpretation, which includes a number of important areas to cover, such as image quality, airway, breathing, cardiac, diaphragm and other.
Under airway, it is necessary to refer to the trachea, carina and bronchi as well as the helar structures.
For breathing, information related to lung fields and pleura is essential.
In the case that no abnormalities are observed, that should be noted as well.
There is no time for me to go into the specifics for the other three areas at this time, but
I'm leaving information as well as an example of documentation for everyone to review.
The final two parts are your overall impression of the chest x-ray, as well as the plan based
on the findings. The plan should be as detailed as possible, including further investigations and
therapies. Many people have left out important details of this part, such as how long a therapy
should last. So please double check this part. Being as specific as possible helps to save time
for the whole team. So... Question 28. You hear part of a ward briefing on history taking and

In light of several instances of missed opportunities when it comes to history taking and information
giving, I wanted to focus on patient communication.
So the framework that you should keep in mind can be easily remembered by the initials ICE.
I-C-E. I stands for ideas, C for concerns and E for expectations. Asking a patient about these
areas enables you to gain insight into how the patient currently perceives their situation,
what they are worried about and what they expect from the interaction. Some questions that you can
use to get at the patient's ideas include, tell me what you think is causing the problem or do you
have any ideas as to what is going on at the moment. These types of questions might lead to
the patient talking about triggers or related symptoms that have not come up before. When it
comes to concerns, questions related to a patient's biggest worry can help to direct treatment so that
it is in line with patient's wants and worries. So the final area of questions includes asking
about expectations related to current problems, such as what you were hoping would happen today.
Similar to concerns, this helps you to get a good idea of the mood of the patient as it relates to…

Welcome, everyone.
As you already know from last week's training, my name is Dr. Padu.
So, last week we covered the horizontal mattress suture, which as you may recall is a useful suture for high tension wounds, especially when the edges are fragile and frayed.
We also looked at the corner stitch, a variation of the horizontal mattress suture, which is commonly used for closure of angled skin flaps and wounds.
So today we're going to do an overview of the vertical mattress suture before going into the
skills lab to get some practice with this useful but somewhat underutilized suture. Some of what
I'm about to say will be the same or similar to what we saw last week with the horizontal mattress
suture but it is always useful to review this information as well as to make sure you understand
the similarities between these suture types. So, the vertical mattress stitch is a suture type
used to close skin wounds. This stitch is used most commonly in anatomic locations prone to
inversion, such as the posterior aspect of the neck and sites of greater skin laxity.
It is also useful for deep lacerations, where it can replace two layers of deep and superficial
sutures. Vertical mattress sutures are not recommended for sites such as the palm of the
hand where important structures lie fairly superficial to the epidermis. As I've already
alluded to, this suture type has a number of advantages such as providing closure for both
deep and superficial layers and also allowing for perfect aversion and vertical opposition of the
superficial skin edges. The disadvantage of this suture type is that it is time-consuming and
unforgiving of operator error, meaning that poor vertical alignment of edges can result in cross
hatching or small scars being left along the main wound. The propensity of the vertical mattress
suture to create cross hatching limits its use in cosmetically sensitive areas such as the face.
To minimize the risk of scarring, the recommended time for removal of this suture is 5-7 days.
If it is deemed necessary to leave the suture in place longer, bolsters may be placed between
the suture and the skin to minimize strangulation of the tissues when the wound swells in response
to post-operative edema. So, just a few reminders about the basic principles of wound management.
First of all, patients should be up to date with their tetanus immunization
and contaminated wounds warrant a course of an antibiotic.
Also, x-rays should be performed if there is any suspicion of a fracture or foreign body.
Finally, wound edges should be debrided if the wound is contaminated
and only if there is no damage deep to the skin can a primary closure be performed.

So, going into the procedure. As with any sterile procedure, once the wound has been treated with a local anesthetic, it, as well as the surrounding skin, must be prepared with an antiseptic solution before placing a drape around the sterile field.
In addition, you must wash your hands and wear sterile gloves, taking care not to desterilize during the procedure.
At this point in the procedure, you should also plan the entry and exit of your suture on either side of the wound.
So, now on to technique.
The vertical mattress stitch is placed in a far, far, near, near order of bites.
The far, far loop passes relatively deeply into the dermis, approximately 7mm,
and the near-near loop enters and exits the skin surface 1-2mm from the wound margin
and traverses the wound at 1mm depth.
It is important to remember that you will reload for the near-near loop with your needle facing away from you
and then throw the suture directly above or superficial your original throw.
Because of the precise degree of control that the vertical mattress stitch provides,
bites must be symmetrical, especially in the near-near loop or the wound will misalign.
Now, the knot is tightened only until sufficient opposition and aversion is achieved.
Overenthusiastic tightening increases the likelihood that the suture material will cut
into the skin during wound healing. Also, the knot will lie to one side of the wound
because you have both suture ends coming from the same side.
So, just to review before going into the skills lab,

So, today in our series on women who shaped medicine, I have the honor to introduce Mrs.
Tu, who is the first mainland Chinese scientist to receive a Nobel Prize in a scientific category,
and she did so without a doctorate, a medical degree or training abroad.
Simply amazing.
So, please receive a warm welcome, Mrs Tu.
Thank you for having me. It's a pleasure to be here.
So, I just gave a bit of information about your background
but it definitely does not tell the whole story.
What inspired you to become a scientist?
Well, education was always important in my family
but the time in my life that had the biggest impact on my future was when I was 16.
I contracted tuberculosis and I had to take a two-year break from studying.
When I eventually returned to school, I knew exactly what I wanted to study, medicine. I was
driven to find cures for disease like that one that had afflicted me. So I studied pharmacology,
including learning how to classify medicinal plants and extract active ingredients and determine their chemical structures.
When I graduated from college, I started working at a newly established institute, the Academy of Traditional Chinese Medicine.
Very interesting, that focus on medicinal plants.
So when did you set your sights on malaria, research that would eventually lead you to the Nobel Prize?
Well, that was in mid-1967 when North Vietnam asked China for help battling the disease
because it was causing tremendous casualties among its soldiers in the war.
The parasite that causes malaria had become resistant to chloroquine,
the standard malaria treatment at the time.
So Chairman Mao Zedong launched a project to find a cure for chloroquine-resistant malaria.
A few years later, I was appointed to head the project.
So how do you even go about taking over such a huge project like this?
Well, my first order of business was researching the effects of malaria in situ.
At the time I took over the project,
Hainan Island in southern China was experiencing a malaria outbreak,
so I travelled there to see for myself the effect of the disease.
So you witnessed first-hand the disease's devastating toll on the human body?
Yes, I did.
When I eventually returned to China, my team started to review ancient medical texts to understand traditional Chinese ways of fighting malaria.
I mean, we had to do something.
At that point, over 240,000 compounds had been tested for use in potential anti-malarial drugs and none had worked.
Eventually, we found a reference to sweet wormwood,
which had been used in China around 400 AD
to treat what was intermittent fevers in the text.
Ah, I see. Intermittent fevers are a symptom of malaria.
Exactly. Once we knew what we were looking for,
it didn't take us that long to isolate one active compound in wormwood
that seemed to battle malaria-friendly parasites.
We tested the extracts of the compound, but nothing worked.
so we went back to the ancient texts. What were you looking for exactly? Well I wondered whether
the active ingredient in wormwood was being damaged when we boiled it to preserve the solvent
so I tried another preparation this time with an ether-based solvent which boils at a lower
temperature. This preparation didn't damage the wormwood. Animal testing showed a 100% success
test rate with this new preparation. That is amazing. 100% test rate. So how did human testings go?
How did human testing go? Well, actually, two colleagues and myself were the first human test
subjects. And then we tested it on 21 patients in Hainan province. The good news is all of us
recovered. That is definitely dedication to one's work. So when things calmed down,
what was found to be the compound's active ingredient? The active ingredient is called
artemisinin. I think of it as a gift from traditional Chinese medicine to the world.
It truly is. And how did you feel about the amount of time it took for the World Health
Organization to recommend artemisinin combination therapy as a first line of defence against malaria?
Well, it did take us a few years to get our work published in English, so there is that.
I mean, the WHO, World Bank and UN became interested in our findings soon after that.
So I guess what I'm trying to say is the important thing is that patients started to receive effective treatment.
